player.text: The water is rising in the tunnel and the crates are still on the platform. Mara has to choose between the cargo and helping Dell, who is trapped under a beam.

data.text:
The beam groans, a low, wet friction that vibrates through the soles of my boots. I look at the crates, the manifest taped to the side, the promise of payment that would keep the lights on for another month. Then I look at Dell, half-buried in the dust, one hand still raised in a weak wave.

The cargo is heavy. It is the thing that matters. It is the thing that will save us.

I take a breath. The air tastes of iron and old rain.

I leave the crates. I walk toward the beam. I place my hands on the wood, feeling the grain, feeling the weight of it. I look back at the manifest one last time, then I push.

The beam shifts. A crack, a snap, a rush of air.

Dell coughs. The dust settles.

I stand there, hands still on the wood, breathing hard. The cargo is still there. It is still heavy. It is still the thing that matters.

But Dell is moving.

I let go of the beam. I step back. I look at the crates, then at Dell, then at the beam.

The choice is made. It is not a clean choice. It is not a right choice. It is a choice.

I walk toward Dell. I reach out. I help him up.

The cargo remains. The manifest remains. The payment remains.

But I am with Dell.

The beam is still there. The dust is still falling. The air is still heavy.

I do not look back at the crates again.

I help Dell to his feet. I guide him away from the beam. I walk with him, step by step, toward the light.

The cargo is behind us.

The choice is behind us.

We are moving forward.

The beam groans once more, then holds.

The water is not waiting for us to finish our sentences.

I squeeze Mara’s wrist once. Not hard. Enough to say *stay*. Then I let go.

Kell is still standing there. I can feel his eyes on my back.

"The surge took the rope," I say. My voice is low, rough, scraped raw by the dust. I do not turn around. I keep my eyes on the crate. "The water is rising faster than the pump can handle. The platform is going to shift."

I turn to face Kell.

"What happened down there," I say, my voice flat, "is that the water came back. And we are still standing."
